facts.title: Discovered in 15 days
facts.text: Neon was discovered in London in June 1898 by Scottish chemist William Ramsay and his assistant Morris Travers. They found it by chilling air into a liquid and slowly boiling it off, capturing a leftover gas after argon, krypton, and xenon. Travers later wrote that the brilliant crimson glow it gave off in a discharge tube 'told its own story and was a sight to dwell upon and never to forget.'

facts.title: Named by a curious child
facts.text: The name comes from the Greek word 'neos,' meaning 'new.' According to Travers, it was Ramsay's 13-year-old son Willie who suggested calling the new element 'novum,' which his father adapted into the Greek-rooted 'neon.' The choice fit, since it was the freshest addition to the newly minted family of noble gases.

facts.title: The signature red glow
facts.text: The familiar red-orange light of 'neon signs' is true neon's natural color when an electric current excites its atoms. Pure neon in a glass tube emits a distinctive reddish-orange light at wavelengths near 640 nanometers. Other colors seen in commercial signs actually come from different gases or coated tubes, so a genuinely red sign is the only one truly powered by neon.

facts.title: Almost impossible to react
facts.text: Neon is the most inert of all the elements, with chemists never having made a single stable, ordinary chemical compound of it. Its outer electron shell is completely full, and it holds its electrons so tightly that it resists bonding even with the most aggressive reactants like fluorine. This extreme reluctance makes neon, in practical terms, the most chemically unreactive substance known.

facts.title: Brighter than its noble cousins
facts.text: For a given electrical input, a neon discharge produces far more intense light than the other noble gases, which is why it became the workhorse of luminous tube lighting. French engineer Georges Claude exploited this, displaying the first neon lamp in Paris in December 1910 and the first neon advertising sign by 1912. His company Claude Neon went on to sell the technology worldwide.

facts.title: Rare on Earth, abundant in stars
facts.text: Neon is the fifth most abundant element in the entire universe, yet it makes up only about 18 parts per million of Earth's atmosphere. The mismatch exists because neon is so light and unreactive that early Earth's gravity could not hold onto it, letting most of it escape to space. In stars, neon is forged during the late 'neon-burning' stage of massive stellar evolution shortly before they explode.

facts.title: A super-cold refrigerant
facts.text: Liquid neon is a remarkably powerful coolant, with more than 40 times the refrigerating capacity per unit volume of liquid helium and over three times that of liquid hydrogen. It boils at about minus 246 degrees Celsius, just 27 degrees above absolute zero. This makes it valuable for cryogenics where engineers need intense cooling without the extreme expense and handling difficulty of liquid helium.

facts.title: Three stable isotopes
facts.text: Natural neon is a mix of three stable isotopes: neon-20 makes up about 90.5 percent, neon-22 about 9.3 percent, and neon-21 a tiny 0.27 percent. Studying the precise ratios of these isotopes in volcanic rocks and meteorites lets geologists trace material that came from deep within the Earth's mantle. Such 'neon fingerprints' are key evidence in understanding how our planet first acquired its gases.

facts.title: No role in life
facts.text: Despite being all around us in the air we breathe, neon plays no known biological role in any living organism. It is completely non-toxic and chemically harmless, simply passing in and out of the lungs without taking part in any process. The only real danger it poses is as a simple asphyxiant, since a room flooded with neon would displace the oxygen needed to breathe.

facts.title: A discharge-tube workhorse
facts.text: Beyond advertising, neon's reliable glow made it useful in voltage testers, high-voltage indicators, and the little orange pilot lamps once common in electronics. Because neon ionizes at a predictable voltage, tiny neon bulbs were used as simple indicators and even as components in early electronic logic and timing circuits. Neon is also mixed into helium-neon lasers, which produced the steady red beams used for decades in supermarket barcode scanners.
